input.question: How was knowledge ‘lost’ after the fall of Rome?
input.ground_truth: In addition to the excellent answers we've got here, in [this thread](_URL_0_), /u/Tiako and /u/bitparity discuss quality of life after the fall of the Roman Empire, which, will not a strict answer to OP's question, certainly has a lot of overlap and will probably prove to be of interest.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

I am a woman.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How was knowledge ‘lost’ after the fall of Rome?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big box full of your favorite toys and storybooks. This box is like all the knowledge people in Rome had—like how to build roads, write stories, and do math.

But then, something big happens, like if your house gets messy and some toys get lost or broken. When Rome stopped being the big, strong country it was (that’s what “the fall of Rome” means), lots of people moved away or things got mixed up.

Some of the grown-ups who knew how to read and write left, or they didn’t write down everything they knew anymore. Some books got old and fell apart. Some people forgot how to make certain things because they didn’t have anyone to teach them.

So, just like you might lose some of your toys or forget how to play a game if no one shows you, people after the fall of Rome lost a lot of their knowledge because it wasn’t written down, or the people who knew it were gone, or things got mixed up and broken.

That’s how knowledge got “lost” after Rome fell.
